statement: Seven whole numbers add up to 50. At most how many of them can be odd?

choices.misconception: I thought an even total means every one of the numbers has to be even.
I thought at most half of the seven numbers can be odd, and rounded down.
I thought the number of odd numbers has to be odd, so I took the largest odd count below 7.
I did not check the parity: seven odd numbers always add up to an odd total, never 50.

hints: What kind of total do you get from an odd number of odd numbers?
A sum of whole numbers is even exactly when it contains an even number of odd terms. So the count of odd numbers here must be even, and it cannot be more than 7.
The count of odd numbers must be even and at most 7. Test whether 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1 and 44 works.

solutions.reliable: A sum is even only when it contains an even number of odd terms. Since 50 is even, the number of odd numbers is even, so 7 is impossible and the most is 6. Six odd numbers really do work: 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 44 = 50. The transferable idea: parity often rules out the obvious answer, and then a single example shows the next one is possible.

whyOnTest: Parity questions test that the number of odd terms decides whether a sum is odd or even.
